zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). The supplied native BnF scan remains the authority for text, typeface and physical placement.

lines.note: The opening continues the preceding page's Japanese statement about a fault: qua to yuu means 'call it a fault'. The Portuguese distinguishes making an error from failing to correct it; the scan supports Errar and the negative não, not OCR Erar and mão.

runs.text: ro, ißo he o que ſe chama peccado.

lines.note: Ro completes erro across the physical break. The gloss concludes that the uncorrected error is what is called a sin; retain the printed peccado rather than modernizing it.
Quabi denotes beauty or splendour, as shown by fermoſa and lustroſa. Vt introduces the literary example below; the aligned draft's st allograph in lustroſa is retained rather than globally recast.
The phrase quabi xenqen nari characterizes conspicuous beauty or brilliance. Its Portuguese rendering, 'it is a beautiful and ... thing', continues on the next row.
Fermoſa completes the paired description bella and fermoſa. The following S. is an upright written-register label, not part of the italic Portuguese adjective.
Quabita fito is a splendidly or elegantly dressed person. The Portuguese ga- begins galante on the next line; the example is Japanese, whereas Vt is italic apparatus.
Lante completes galante, followed by 'splendidly dressed'. This describes the person's appearance rather than a separate sense of the following peace-making headword.
Quabocu here is peace or a truce, corresponding to waboku. The repeated example is divided Qua-/bocu; the printed hyphen is visible at the column edge.
Bocu completes Quabocu, and suru turns the noun into 'make peace'. The Portuguese also gives establishing friendship as an equivalent.
This homograph is a flowering tree, not the preceding peace or truce. Hana no ki and aruore florida agree; the damaged capital does not justify the OCR's isolated Q.
The relative clause ends 'gives flowers', completing the flowering-tree definition. The grave on dà is retained as printed.
Bun ni suguru explains exceeding one's allotted measure or station; the Portuguese emphasizes abundance. This prepares the appreciative use in the following related entries.
Copia completes the paired gloss for abundance or plenty. The scan supports one Portuguese word, not the OCR's co pia.
Quabunna is the adjectival form, describing something abundant or great. Itẽ introduces an additional figurative or transferred use continued below.

runs.text: per met. Palaura de agradecer, & ter em

lines.note: The abbreviated per met. introduces a transferred expression of gratitude or high valuation. Ter em is completed by muito on the next row; the abbreviation is not expanded in the text.
Muito completes ter em muito, 'esteem highly'. This short physical row closes the appreciative sense rather than beginning the adverb below.
Quabunni is the adverbial form, glossed as abundantly or greatly. The printed Abundamente is retained without inserting the extra syllable of modern abundantemente.
To completes muito; quabunni zonzuru illustrates grateful appreciation. Zonzuru is the Japanese verb in the example, not part of the Portuguese infinitive Agradecer.
The alternative Portuguese rendering is 'esteem very highly'. It completes the same appreciative example and supports the transferred sense noted above.
Quaccǒ names an aromatic medicinal substance. The gloss does not identify a botanical species, so none is supplied; the downward vowel mark is retained as ǒ.
Hana and tori identify flowers and birds, agreeing directly with the Portuguese pair. Reinspection recovers the c lost in OCR Quahô and retains the upward circumflex.

The festival or calendrical expression is explained as the first day of the second month. Preserve the printed Quachô spelling and the checked endings in xet and Niguat rather than regularizing them from a modern calendar term.
The Portuguese explicitly says the first day of the second lunar month. This is the dictionary's stated date, not a date silently reconciled with other calendrical traditions.
Hi no naka means in the midst of fire, exactly matching no meyo do fogo. This fire compound must remain distinct from the flowers compound immediately below.

runs.text: Entre as roſas, ou no meyo das ro-

lines.note: This Quachǔ means among roses or flowers, contrasting with the preceding fire compound. The scan visibly ends ro- even though the next row repeats roſas; that compositor's repetition is preserved.
The row prints the whole word roſas followed by 'or flowers'. It is not reduced to ſas merely to repair the preceding ro-; the duplicated syllable is a source anomaly.
Quaco is the past, with sugi and saru explaining passing away. The Portuguese begins 'time or age' and supplies paßado on the next row.
The three Japanese terms are past, present, and future. Guenzai retains the dictionary's gue spelling; the sequence also recurs later on this page.
This is the Portuguese translation of the preceding three-part temporal sequence. Each adjective corresponds in order to quaco, guenzai, and mirai.
Quacqei denotes a comfortable, enjoyable way of life or pastime. The example is divided Quac-/qei, with a visible terminal hyphen.
The completed quacqei suru means to lead a good or comfortable life. The historic Portuguese Leuar is retained, not modernized to levar.

runs.text: Couſa de boa vida, & paßa tẽ-

lines.note: The adjectival form describes something associated with an easy life and recreation. Tẽ- begins the abbreviated Portuguese word for time across the line break.

Po completes tẽpo; quacqeina fito describes a man living at ease. The following deſcã- starts the Portuguese word for being rested or at ease, retaining its printed nasal abbreviation across the physical break.

runs.text: ſado, & que ſe leua boa vida.

lines.note: The gloss finishes 'at ease, and who leads a good life'. The printed reflexive-looking ſe in the Portuguese is retained rather than silently regularized.
This row supplies the adverbial derivative and labels it Adu. Its meaning is inherited from the preceding comfortable-life entries; the print gives no additional translation to fill in.
Tsuru muragaru describes cranes flocking together. Bando de begins the equivalent Portuguese expression for a flock of cranes.
Grous completes the flock-of-cranes gloss. The following S. is an upright written-register label despite the damaged type.

Akirakana koto identifies something clear or evident. Enlargement supports the abbreviation mark on final e, read as ẽ; Quacujen below and supplied NINJAL 203a18 corroborate Quacujẽ, without replacing its printed abbreviated form.
Quacumei likewise denotes something clear and manifest. The scan supports the single word manifesta rather than OCR mani festa; its aligned st classification is retained. S. remains upright.
The alternative marker l introduces Quacujen, and Idem refers back to the same clear-or-manifest sense. The two Japanese variants remain separately printed forms.
Quacuran is equated with the historical illness-name mordexim. The scan gives an abbreviated Doẽça; no modern diagnosis is inserted. Qua- begins the following example.
The example says quacuran wo shita, followed by an alternative quacuranqena expression. The Portuguese infinitive Eſtar begins the statement that the person is suffering from the named illness.
This completes 'be afflicted with mordexim'. It belongs with both Japanese expressions above and is a complete short continuation row.

Tsuru no tsubasa identifies cranes' wings. The damaged middle of the headword is read Quacurei, rather than OCR Quararei; surviving strokes and supplied NINJAL 203a22 support this choice, but the internal damaged letters remain a nonblocking caveat.
Grou completes the crane-wing definition. The upright S. marks the word's written register.
Hi no ana is a pit of fire, rendered as a fiery cavern and then hell. The Portuguese word has an f, not the OCR's long-s reading ſogo; the final t in Quacut remains a checked coda.

Tatara no yu identifies molten metal associated with the furnace. The internally damaged headword is read Quacutǒ, supported by its surviving types and supplied NINJAL 203a24; the internal u remains less secure. Metal corrects OCR Meial, while der- begins derretido below.
Retido completes derretido: metal melted in the fire. The physical row closes the column, above the bottom rule, and is not page furniture.

runs.text: Odio, ou maleuolencia que hum tẽ

lines.note: Quacuxu denotes hatred or ill will held against someone. The abbreviated tẽ belongs to the Portuguese verb and continues with the location of that resentment below.
The resentment is held 'in the heart against someone'. This finishes the definition, not a new example or entry.
Tsuru no tsubasa literally gives cranes' wings. The following explanation extends this image to a military arrangement rather than stopping at the literal anatomical meaning.

runs.text: grou: tomaſe por hum certo modo de por em ordẽ

lines.note: The crane-wing term is used for a particular manner of putting forces in order. The visible colon introduces the transferred use; ordẽ remains abbreviated.
The object is an army placed in battle order. This completes the military sense of Quacuyocu without supplying an unprinted description of the formation.
Quadai is the element of fire. The definition concerns an elemental category, not merely an individual flame.
Quadan denotes planted beds or containers for herbs and flowers, as indicated by alegretes. The list of plants continues below.
Flores completes the alternative to roses in the garden-bed definition. This single-word continuation is retained as its own physical row.
Uribatake is a melon field, agreeing with meloal. The Portuguese ſe- begins ſemeado, describing how the field is planted.
Meado completes ſemeado: a field sown with melons. The nasal mark in melões is retained on the printed vowel.

Hana no tateyoo wo shiruitaru describes a text recording how to arrange flowers. The final xo on the next row completes the noun for the written work; xiruitaru is retained as the historical form, not modernized to shirushitaru.

runs.text: Liuro que enſina a concertar flores, ou

lines.note: Xo completes the Japanese explanatory phrase. The Portuguese defines a book teaching the arranging of flowers; concertar is not silently modernized or confused with a musical concert here.

runs.text: roſas em algum vaſo, como ramalhetes.

lines.note: The flowers or roses are arranged in a vessel, like bouquets. This completes the first definition of the book.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Liuro que trata do modo de fazer

lines.note: Item begins a second book-related meaning, distinct from arranging flowers. The sentence introduces instruction in the activities listed on the next row.
The second book treats performance of plays, instrumental playing, and singing. The print does not specify a particular surviving title, so none is inserted.
Bonai no quado illustrates excess in marital relations. The Portuguese begins 'fault or ...', with the nature of the excess explained in the following two rows.

runs.text: demaſia q̃ cometem os caſados em vſar frequẽte

lines.note: The gloss describes the excess committed by married people in frequent sexual relations. The line ends frequẽte without a visible hyphen; the continuation alone is not grounds for adding one.
Mente completes the adverb frequently, followed by the marital act. This is the historical dictionary's evaluation, not a present-day recommendation.

runs.text: A mayor parte, ou mais da metade.

lines.note: Quafan denotes the greater part or more than half. The two Portuguese formulations establish the quantitative sense.
Hi no hotori means beside the fire. Apar is retained as the printed close spelling of the Portuguese expression 'alongside', rather than divided from modern preference.
Quafin is a flower vase or arrangement likened to a bouquet. The scan and baseline support coma, although como would be the expected comparative; the anomalous final vowel is retained.
Quafô is good fortune or blessed happiness. The upward circumflex is retained and carried into the visibly matching derivatives, not replaced by a generic long-vowel mark.
Quafô imijii hito describes a person with exceptional good fortune. The Portuguese calls him fortunate and continues with bemauenturado below.
After completing the fortunate-person gloss, quafô tsutanai supplies the contrasting case of poor fortune. Ho- starts Homem on the next physical line.
The second example describes an unfortunate, ill-fated person. It is the opposite of the preceding imijij example, not a new headword.
The adjectival derivative describes something fortunate or blessed. The following Item extends that description to a person.
The additional gloss is a fortunate, well-favoured person. Peßoa preserves the printed double-s sort rather than modern pessoa.
Feliz supplies the final equivalent, happy or fortunate. The short continuation completes Quafôna before its derivative forms below.
This indented derivative is the adverbial form of Quafôna. The scan supplies no separate Portuguese gloss, so the transcription leaves it as a standalone printed form.
This indented derivative expresses the quality or degree of good fortune. It belongs with the preceding adjective and adverb; no missing definition is invented.
Quafôxa denotes a fortunate person. The Portuguese repeats the prosperous or well-favoured characterization, distinct from the abstract derivative above.
Hi and kaze explain fire and wind. The final caron on u is preserved as a printed long-vowel mark, not interpreted through the separate long-o contrast.
Wazawai and saiwai supply misfortune and good fortune. The Portuguese begins the same bad-and-good contrast, with the grave in mà retained.
Boa completes the contrast, then the gloss restates it as evils and prosperity. This is a paired abstract expression, not two independent entries.
Quafuguiǔ contrasts exceeding the measure with falling short. The scan shows one roman headword; OCR wrongly made its damaged initial an italic O. Yo- begins Yorozzuni below.
Yorozzuni quafugyuu wa warui says that excess and deficiency are bad in everything. The Japanese topic particle remains attached as printed; Portuguese a- begins auer below.

runs.text: uer demaſia, ou falta he ruim.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes 'to have excess or deficiency is bad'. This is the translation of the preceding general maxim, not an additional definition.
Quaguei is a bell that is sounded. The gloss provides no narrower identification of its material or ceremonial use.
Quaguenmi compresses the three time categories quaco, guenzai, and mirai. The Portuguese pre- begins preterito on the following row.
The completed gloss is past, present, and future, in the same order as the Japanese expansion. It recalls the fuller Quaco example in column 1.
Hana and tsuki explain flowers and the moon. The final t of Quaguet is preserved as the printed checked ending.
The moon completes the flowers-and-moon pair. The S. is upright written-register apparatus rather than italic Portuguese.
Catatçuburi identifies a snail and agrees with caracol. Preserve this Japanese variant rather than substituting a modern standard form.
Suguru nochi means after something has passed. The headword is Quago, not OCR Qi ago, and the verb's g is supported by its descender rather than the OCR's cedilla reading.

Zocuquago no chookyuu introduces the image of drawing a bow only after the thief has gone. The Portuguese Ar- begins armar. The final u-mark in chǒqiù is faint; the aligned draft's grave is retained as the chosen reading, with its exact shape a nonblocking caveat.

runs.text: mar o arco depois do ladrão acolhido. i, Acu-

lines.note: The bow is readied after the thief has escaped or taken shelter. Acu- starts the explicit interpretation of the proverb on the next row.

The gloss ends with bringing the remedy too late. Enlargement shows a modest but visible word gap between dir and tarde, so the OCR's joined dirtarde is separated; dir completes acu- on the preceding physical row.
